components.text: Contacts the demand for a secular moral standard by identifying flourishing and unnecessary suffering as the substantive objects of inquiry.
Does not yet establish why the adopted welfare aim is universally binding rather than selected.
Whether secular morality can specify a substantive evaluative aim rather than inherit a divine standard.
Whether selecting welfare supplies universally binding truth or obligation rather than merely a chosen definition.
Offers God's nature and essence as a nonarbitrary moral standard in place of a merely selected definition.
Does not directly show why a character-based standard defeats the secular distinction between choosing a standard and objectively applying it.
Whether morality has a nonarbitrary standard beyond a humanly selected welfare definition.
Whether divine self-revelation makes moral requirements epistemically accessible.
Directly challenges whether immutability explains why God has this moral nature rather than a contrary eternal nature.
Whether immutability explains why God has this moral nature rather than an eternally contrary nature.
Whether a mind-grounded standard is thereby nonarbitrary and necessary.
Rejects the contrary-nature hypothetical on the ground that changing God's essential holiness changes the subject.
Does not explain why the actual essential nature is good or uniquely possible.
Whether an imagined being with contrary essential traits would still be the God whose nature grounds morality.
Whether God's revealed actual character supplies a moral standard.
Directly argues that identifying God as the sole standard makes the evaluation of God's goodness circular.
Explains that refusing the counterfactual does not supply an independent basis for evaluating the standard.
Whether God's nature can be evaluated as good without using that same nature as the sole standard.
Whether rejecting contrary divine character resolves the circular evaluation problem.
Whether a mind-grounded source is thereby nonarbitrary.
Challenges the move from conformity to God's nature to a rational reason for human obedience.
Uses the absence of an external evaluation to argue that the practical authority claim remains unsupported.
Whether conformity to God's own nature supplies a noncircular rational reason for human obedience.
Whether actual divine identity answers the practical reason-for-obedience problem.
Offers divine omniscience as a reason to trust that revelations rest on considerations unavailable to limited agents.
Does not explain why superior information makes the revealer morally good or authoritative.
Whether divine guidance may rest on reasons unavailable to epistemically limited human agents.
Whether omniscience independently establishes that God's underlying reasons are morally good.
Argues that complete consequence knowledge enables informed prescriptions and thus supplies an epistemic reason for deference.
Does not establish that consequences or knowledge make God the ontological moral standard.
Whether God can provide informed action guidance unavailable to limited human reasoners.
Whether consequence knowledge makes God the moral foundation rather than a superior evaluator.
Identifies that complete knowledge explains reliable transmission of consequence facts, not what makes an action right, and states the intermediary consequence.
Concedes that limited humans might rationally defer to an omniscient source for information.
Whether omniscient consequence knowledge makes God the moral standard rather than an informational intermediary.
Whether hidden divine reasons establish metaphysical grounding rather than epistemic access.
Directly answers the truth-value challenge by distinguishing selection of a standard from objective truth under that standard.
Shows that objective evaluation need not require a divine evaluator, though it does not establish categorical obligation.
Whether objective truth can exist in judgments made against a conventionally selected standard.
Whether accurate application requires a uniquely divine evaluator.
Rejects the chosen-standard account as unable to justify moral absolutes and invokes an eliminative theistic alternative.
Challenges whether secular welfare can account for universal moral truth.
Does not answer the circularity objection to the remaining theistic option.
Whether a chosen secular standard can account for moral absolutes rather than merely conditional measurements.
Whether atheistic welfare accounts exhaust the alternatives to divine grounding.
Whether defeating one secular account independently validates divine grounding.
Offers a purported universal moral truth and a revealed divine standard as more than objective application under convention.
Uses an extreme case compatible with welfare reasoning but does not distinguish divine revelation from the secular basis in that case.
Whether at least one moral judgment is universally true rather than merely conditional on a selected convention.
Whether revelation explains why the torture prohibition is true.
Tests whether a simplified harm criterion can condemn a secret assault when stipulated downstream harms are absent.
Does not show that richer secular standards cannot include autonomy, risk, rule effects, or potential states.
Whether a welfare or harm criterion preserves condemnation when stipulated immediate harms and awareness are absent.
Whether the scenario eliminates potential, rights-based, dispositional, and rule-level harms.
Expands the secular criterion beyond immediate experienced harm to actual and potential conscious states and rule consequences.
Explains how secular reasoning can preserve strongly shared verdicts through broader consequences.
Whether secular evaluation should include potential conscious states and rule-level consequences rather than immediate experienced harm alone.
Whether welfare-sensitive rules can preserve strong prohibitions without revelation.
Whether sophisticated secular consequence reasoning remains a viable alternative.
Provides an impartial rule-construction method capable of rejecting permission for assault without relying on the victim's later awareness.
Supplies a secular alternative to the asserted two-option elimination.
Offers an impartial procedure that can support universal prohibitions.
Whether a secular procedure can justify impartial rules without presupposing divine authority.
Whether impartial agents would accept rules permitting hidden assaults.
Whether universally protective rules can be justified contractually.
Does not address impartial hypothetical agreement; it substitutes an individual recipient-preference criterion.
Does not engage actual and potential states or rule-level consequences.
Whether impartial rule construction avoids dependence on any particular recipient's immediate preferences.
Whether the secular account evaluates potential states and rule-level consequences rather than recipient preference alone.
Whether a simple recipient-preference account can assign variable evaluations.
Recasts the contrary-nature hypothetical to expose the consequence of defining morality solely by divine nature.
Shows that the divine account can likewise detach moral status from welfare outcomes.
Challenges whether character identity alone explains goodness.
Whether defining goodness by divine nature permits a contrary nature that makes universal misery morally good.
Whether actual immutability independently explains the goodness of the divine nature.
Whether the divine account has an advantage in preserving welfare-sensitive judgments.
Grants the objective prohibition and asks what motivational reason follows for an agent who believes it but intends to violate it.
Grants the Christian factual framework while separating belief in revelation from motivation to comply.
Whether belief that a divine prohibition is objectively true necessarily supplies motivation to comply.
Whether accepting divine omniscience itself motivates obedience.
Whether moral truth and practical motivation are distinct issues.
Identifies that inconsistent practice does not entail the absence of objective moral truth and states the truth-compliance distinction.
Does not supply the motivating reason the opponent requested.
Whether failure to comply with acknowledged moral truth undermines the existence of objective moral requirements.
Whether the content of the divine standard is independently good.
Claims Christianity contains prescriptions and therefore can state an ought where atheistic descriptions cannot.
Does not explain why the Christian prescription is rationally binding rather than merely asserted.
Does not address whether divine prescriptions could track a harmful stipulated nature.
What reason makes a divine prescription binding or motivating for an agent who accepts all Christian descriptions.
Whether merely stating a prescription supplies a noncircular reason for obedience.
Whether secular descriptions alone entail categorical prescriptions.
Identifies that listing divine facts and even calling God the standard does not entail a duty, and states the missing-bridge consequence.
Preserves the distinction between truth and compliance while asking for the separate reason to obey.
Treats omnipotence, punishment, and related divine facts as insufficient without a normative premise.
Whether divine creation, power, standard-setting, and punishment entail a duty to obey.
Whether objective truth alone supplies an agent-relative reason to comply.
Whether description of divine nature itself yields normative authority.
Supplies an explicit proposed reason: right conduct glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and moral standard.
Does not independently explain why glorifying or conforming to God is a reason binding every agent.
What normative consideration is offered as the reason agents ought to act consistently with God.
Why God's being the right standard is not circularly assumed in the reason for obedience.
Whether divine glory necessarily motivates an agent who accepts the factual claims.
